about.t: Runs Indiana's election administration, business filings and securities regulation. The top two finishers also set which parties get major-party ballot access.
Outgoing Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales, criticized for travel spending and other conduct, lost his party's nomination to Max Engling at the June 2026 convention.
Engling and Bayh both back Indiana's voter ID law and longer early-voting hours, and both say the next secretary should look into Morales's office. Rated a tossup.

positions.t: Republican.
Backs the federal SAVE Act to verify voters' citizenship and color-coded state IDs so legal noncitizens can't use them to vote.
Has never held elected office: a dozen years as a U.S. House Republican staffer (including for Speaker Kevin McCarthy), then regional director for Sen. Jim Banks; lost a 2024 congressional primary.
Says property taxes should come down while local governments stay funded 'in a fiscally efficient' way.
Wants to cut 'unnecessary red tape' for businesses while screening out fraudulent shell companies.

notes.t: Top stated priority: close Indiana's open primaries so voters can't cross over to the other party's ballot.
Proposes a state inspector general review of the office rather than an outside audit, and a 'Transparency Portal' for reporting election concerns.

positions.t: Democrat.
Wants more early-voting access to raise turnout.
Wants citizen-led ballot initiatives, which Indiana doesn't allow today.
First run for office; son of former Gov. and Sen. Evan Bayh. Republicans criticized his years voting in Indiana while living elsewhere.

notes.t: Pledges an independent audit of the office on day one, with any illegality sent to prosecutors.

Opposes mid-decade redistricting. Wants to cut the gas tax and end the sales tax on utilities. Wants to end straight-ticket voting. Would work with county clerks to flag and remove ineligible voters, and criticized officials for prosecuting only one of 21 noncitizen voters identified.

positions.t: Criticized Morales for handing Indiana's voter rolls to the federal administration, citing voters' privacy.

notes.t: Hamilton County Libertarian chair and University of Indianapolis creative director. Wants a modern state website and voter guide showing who funds every politician, and a neutral office. Opposes mid-decade redistricting. Polling in low single digits.
At the August debate, said voter intent should come first when counting ballots.

positions.t: Former two-term Republican mayor of Indianapolis, now running on the new Lincoln Party line.

notes.t: Pledges not to endorse, donate to or raise money for any candidate whose election his office oversees. Retired Marine lieutenant colonel.
Promises a nonpartisan, low-key office and a nonpartisan state voter guide. Supports independent redistricting commissions and open primaries, and opposed the 2025 mid-decade redistricting push.
The Lincoln Party has no detailed platform yet; Engling has criticized it for that.

about.t: Keeps the state's books, pays its 30,000 employees, sends money to agencies and local governments, and runs the deferred compensation fund.

positions.t: Republican.
With the treasurer, leads a coalition of state financial officers urging Congress to adopt a balanced-budget amendment like Indiana's.
Incumbent; appointed by Gov. Eric Holcomb in December 2023.

notes.t: Priorities: training government finance staff through university partnerships, and the state's transparency portal and federal-funds dashboard.

positions.t: Democrat.
Porter County Clerk; first statewide run.

notes.t: Wants the transparency portal easier to use so residents can find contracts, vendor payments and salaries, and wants spending on housing, child care and affordability programs to carry clear accountability.

positions.t: Has called for reducing government spending.

notes.t: Wants the office run independently of the governor and legislature. Has run for comptroller before; didn't answer the Capital Chronicle survey.

about.t: Invests state money and runs programs such as the college savings plan. The office doesn't write the budget or set tax rates.

contests.title: Allow judges to deny bail in more cases
contests.label: Public Question #1: Ratification of State Constitutional Amendment (Article 1, Section 17)

ballotText.t: Currently, under the Constitution of the State of Indiana, a person charged with murder or treason is not entitled to be released on bail if the proof is evident or the presumption strong. Shall the Constitution of the State of Indiana be amended to provide that a person charged with an offense other than murder or treason is not entitled to bail if: (1) the proof is evident or the presumption strong; and (2) the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect the safety of any other person or the community. (This question concerns Article 1, Section 17 of the Constitution of the State of Indiana.)

summary.t: Today Indiana's constitution lets judges hold someone without bail only for murder or treason. A Yes vote lets judges also deny bail for any other charge when the proof is strong and prosecutors show by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions would keep others safe.
It doesn't list which offenses qualify. Prosecutors' council research says 22 other states have narrowed the right to bail in some way.

contests.yes: Judges can hold people charged with any offense without bail if the court finds no release conditions would keep others safe.
contests.no: Bail stays guaranteed for every charge except murder and treason.

fiscal.t: No official cost estimate was found. Public defenders warn that more people held before trial would add to crowded county jails, which can lead to new jail construction.

pro.t: Prosecutors and sponsors say judges are now forced to release people who pose clear risks, including people who commit violent crimes while out on bail, and that the clear-and-convincing standard is a high bar. An Allen County prosecutor says it's aimed at holding people charged with crimes like attempted murder.

con.t: The ACLU of Indiana says judges already have tools (bail amounts, supervision, no-contact orders, electronic monitoring), that the wording is too broad, and that people could spend months in jail without a conviction, with the burden falling hardest on marginalized communities.

supporters.t: Passed the Senate 43-2 and the House 75-11. Every Republican voted yes; Democrats split. Supporters: county prosecutors. Opponents: ACLU of Indiana, public defenders.

tags.why: Yes widens pretrial detention, a tougher-enforcement step.

quality.t: The amendment covers every offense, not a list of violent crimes as some states use. Lawmakers rejected a change that would have excluded misdemeanors and Level 6 felonies, and Sen. Rodney Pol questioned whether the ballot wording shows how broadly it could apply.
No official estimate of extra jail costs was published for voters.

contests.title: Let city and town court judges live in a neighboring county
contests.label: Public Question #2: Ratification of State Constitutional Amendment (Article 6, Section 6)

ballotText.t: Shall the Constitution of the State of Indiana be amended to permit the judge of a city or town court to reside in: (1) the county in which the court is located; or (2) the bordering county closest to the city or town in which the court is located? (This question concerns Article 6, Section 6 of the Constitution of the State of Indiana.)

summary.t: City and town court judges could live anywhere in the court's county, or in the bordering county closest to the city or town.
Sources differ on today's rule: Ballotpedia says judges must live in the city or town they serve; the courts' legislative update describes a county requirement.

contests.yes: City and town court judges may live in the court's county or the closest bordering county.
contests.no: The current residency rule for city and town court judges stays.

pro.t: Sponsor Rep. Michael Aylesworth says it eases a rural judge shortage; Indiana has about 2.3 lawyers per 1,000 residents.

con.t: Judges could live outside the community, and even the county, whose cases they hear. No organized opposition was found.

supporters.t: Approved by two separately elected General Assemblies (2023 and 2025) and placed on the 2026 ballot.
